sections.h2: What is Washington County, Oregon, and where does it sit?
sections.html:
Washington County is the second most populous county in Oregon, with Hillsboro as its county seat, and it lies about 20 miles west of Portland. The Census counted 600,372 residents in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 611,708.

The county covers 726 square miles, mostly in the Tualatin Valley. The Tualatin Mountains (the West Hills) bound it on the east and north, the Chehalem Mountains lie to the south, and the northern Coast Range lies to the west. The Portland Metro urban growth boundary cuts through the middle of the county, which is why parts of it feel like suburbs and parts feel like farmland.

The Provisional Legislature of Oregon created the county in 1843 as Twality District. It was renamed for George Washington in 1849, and the town first called Columbia, later Hillsboro, became the seat in 1850. Beaverton, Tigard, Sherwood, Forest Grove, Cornelius, Banks, Gaston and North Plains are among the other cities.

sections.h2: What drives the economy in Washington County?
sections.html:
The county is the center of Oregon's Silicon Forest, and its tax base reflects that. Intel, Oregon's largest private-sector employer, has its biggest concentration of workers here, mostly in Hillsboro, and Nike has its headquarters in the county. Agriculture, lumber, manufacturing and food processing also contribute.

Getting around is straightforward for a county this size. Interstate 5, Interstate 205, U.S. 26 and Oregon routes 8, 10, 47 and 217 all serve it. TriMet runs buses, MAX light rail and the Westside Express Service commuter train, and Hillsboro Airport handles air travel. Commute access is something buyers weigh, so mention it when you describe the house.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Washington County?
sections.html:
The Department of Assessment and Taxation values property and collects the tax, and it sits at 155 N. First Avenue, Suite 130, in Hillsboro. One office covers appraisal, recording and payment, which keeps a sale simple to coordinate.

The county's statement flyer lists weekday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and a rear drop box with 24-hour access. Confirm current hours before you drive over, since the office closes for holidays.

sections.h2: Where does a Washington County tax dollar go?
sections.html:
Most of the money goes to schools. The county's explanation of Oregon's system splits each tax dollar this way:

RecipientCents per dollar
Education47.38
Cities and special districts32.42
Washington County16.82
Regional governments3.38

The same page says permanent rates were set in 1995 at $5 per $1,000 of real market value for schools and $10 per $1,000 for general government, with voter-approved bonds and local option levies added on top. A recent statement flyer shows what that looks like in practice, with measures such as a Hillsboro police, fire and parks levy and a Beaverton School District levy for teachers. Because levies differ by district, two houses with the same value can get different bills.

sections.h2: How do real market value and assessed value differ?
sections.html:
Your tax is based on assessed value, which is the lower of real market value (RMV) and maximum assessed value (MAV). RMV is the assessor's estimate of the sale price as of January 1, and the county notes there is no cap on it.

MAV rises by no more than 3% a year. The county adds that taxes can still climb by more than 3% if a district approves a new bond or local option levy, or if major renovations were completed before January 1.

sections.h2: What are the Washington County tax dates and payment options?
sections.html:
Washington County tax is due November 15, and statements go out by October 25. You can pay in full or in thirds, and a full payment postmarked or received by the due date earns a 3% discount.

  • Online or by phone, with a convenience fee for ACH or cards.
  • By mail to 155 N. 1st Avenue, Suite 130, MS 8, Hillsboro, OR 97124. The county asks owners not to send cash or staple a check to the stub.
  • In person or at the drop box at the Public Services Building.

Look at the color of the statement. A green statement means the owner pays the bill. A yellow one means a mortgage company or the Oregon Department of Revenue asked for it, and after a purchase, sale or refinance the county tells owners to confirm with the lender that the tax will still be paid. Delinquent amounts show on the statement, are applied to the oldest year first, and a year marked with an asterisk is in foreclosure proceedings.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Washington County property value?
sections.html:
A value appeal goes to the Property Value Appeals Board, formerly called the Board of Property Tax Appeals, and must be filed between the date statements are mailed and December 31. Washington County charges no filing fee, and an attorney is not required.

  • The board hears value appeals for the current year only. It does not hear complaints about the tax amount.
  • Hearings run from the first Monday in February through April 15, and attending is optional.
  • The strongest evidence is a recent sale, a fee appraisal or comparable homes near January 1.
  • After the board rules, an owner can go to the Magistrate Division of the Oregon Tax Court. The Department of Revenue says to file within 30 days of the board's order, and the county lists the court's filing fee at $50.

The county's appeals line is 503-846-3854. The county's flyer says an appeal rests on market value as of January 1 of the tax year.

sections.h2: Does Washington County charge a transfer tax when you sell?
sections.html:
Yes. Washington County charges a transfer tax of one dollar per thousand dollars of selling price, and the county says liability is shared between buyer and seller. On a $500,000 sale, that works out to $500.

The tax or an exemption claim is due within 15 days of the recording date, and a late penalty applies after that. The county lists exemption forms for several situations:

  • Deeds in lieu of foreclosure and court-ordered transfers
  • Trustee's deeds from foreclosure
  • Transfers by gift, devise or inheritance
  • Transfers between spouses under a dissolution or separation order
  • Sales under $13,999

The Recording Division handles all of this at the same Hillsboro address. Ask your title company which form applies, because an inherited house and an ordinary sale are treated differently.

sections.h2: How are property taxes split at closing in Washington County?
sections.html:
The escrow agent calculates each side's share, and the split depends on the date of closing. Oregon's fiscal tax year runs from July 1 to June 30. A Lawyers Title overview explains that for closings from July 1 through mid-October, the seller credits the buyer a prorated share based on the prior year's tax, and the buyer pays when it comes due.

From mid-October through June 30, the seller has usually paid the tax, and the buyer reimburses a portion from the agreed transfer date. The escrow officer also orders payoff demands, and monetary liens are generally cleared through escrow so the buyer receives clear title.

sections.h2: What if taxes or a deferral lien are owed on the house?
sections.html:
Unpaid taxes and deferral liens come out of the sale proceeds or get resolved before closing, so find out the balance early. Oregon's Senior Citizen's Deferral (age 62 or older) and Disabled Citizen's Deferral let the Department of Revenue pay the tax, place a lien on the property and charge 6% interest, and those amounts must be repaid later. A deferred account is noted at the bottom of the statement.

Foreclosure for unpaid tax is slow but real. Under ORS 312.010, real property can be foreclosed once three years have passed since the earliest delinquency. Under ORS 312.120, the county holds property sold to it for two years after the judgment unless it is redeemed. Washington County's page on tax-foreclosed property says the county may keep, transfer or auction what it takes. If you are behind, selling before judgment keeps the house in your hands.

faqs.q: When are Washington County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The main due date is November 15. Statements are mailed by October 25, and a full payment postmarked or received by November 15 earns a 3% discount. You can also pay in thirds.

faqs.q: What is the Washington County real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: It is one dollar per thousand dollars of selling price, and buyer and seller share liability. You must pay it or file an exemption claim within 15 days of the recording date.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Washington County assessment?
faqs.a: File a petition with the Property Value Appeals Board between the date statements are mailed and December 31. There is no filing fee in Washington County, and the appeals line is 503-846-3854.

faqs.q: What does a yellow tax statement mean in Washington County?
faqs.a: A yellow statement means a mortgage company or the Oregon Department of Revenue requested the bill. If you recently bought, sold or refinanced, confirm with your lender that the tax will still be paid.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Washington County house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is normally paid from the proceeds through escrow, and the title company will order the figures. Foreclosure cannot start until three years after the earliest delinquency, so you generally have time to sell.

faqs.q: How is assessed value set for a Washington County house?
faqs.a: Assessed value is the lower of real market value and maximum assessed value, and MAV rises at most 3% a year. Taxes can still climb faster if a district adds a bond or local option levy or if major work was completed before January 1.
